selection_reason: 1) No prior evidence exists, so the critical uncertainty is whether the task is solvable at all and what the performance floor looks like. 2) config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest viable configuration: a single RNA profile reduced by PCA with no aggregation or fusion. It establishes a clean baseline that isolates the raw predictive signal in the RNA data without confounding from encoder choice, profile multiplicity, or cross-modal fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, starting with the cheapest, most interpretable experiment is the most efficient first step: it is fast to train, provides a reference point against which every added complexity (better encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion strategy) can be measured, and avoids prematurely investing in complex multimodal or learned-encoder configurations whose marginal value over a simple PCA baseline is still unknown.
experiment_summary: This first experiment established a baseline using an RNA-only, single-profile model with PCA (2000 components) and no image modality, aggregation, or fusion. The validation accuracy of ~48.5% (F1 ~46.4%) is an initial observation indicating that the raw PCA-reduced RNA signal alone yields modest predictive performance, though it is unclear whether this reflects the ceiling for RNA-only approaches or simply the floor before added complexity. It remains uncertain whether learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or cross-modal fusion could substantially improve beyond this baseline, and whether the task is broadly solvable at higher accuracy levels.

selection_reason: With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → ~48.5% acc), we have zero evidence about whether the image modality carries any independent predictive signal. This is the single most important uncertainty to resolve before investing in any multimodal or fusion configurations. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest, cleanest image-only baseline: it changes exactly one high-level dimension (modality) relative to config_001 while keeping profile setting, aggregation, and fusion at their minimal defaults. If image alone approaches or exceeds the RNA baseline, it confirms the image modality is informative and justifies pursuing multimodal fusion (configs 016–051). If image alone is substantially worse, it tells us to focus the remaining budget on improving the RNA side (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation) rather than spending experiments on multimodal configurations that may not benefit from a weak second modality. This experiment maximizes information gain per trial under a limited budget by resolving a binary, strategy-shaping question that no other single experiment can answer.
experiment_summary: This experiment established an image-only, single-profile baseline using a ResNet50 encoder with no aggregation or fusion, yielding a validation accuracy of ~20.8% (F1 ~17.2%), which is substantially lower than the RNA-only PCA baseline of ~48.5%. This initial observation suggests that, under this configuration, the image modality carries considerably weaker independent predictive signal than the RNA modality, though the comparison is confounded by differing encoder choices (learned ResNet50 vs. linear PCA) and cannot definitively isolate modality as the sole cause of the gap. It remains uncertain whether alternative image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or a different architectural setup could substantially improve the image signal, and whether even a weak image contribution might still add value in a multimodal fusion setting.

selection_reason: Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieved 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) achieved only 20.8% acc. The RNA modality is clearly the stronger signal, but we have no evidence yet on whether the PCA representation is near its ceiling or whether a learned nonlinear encoder could substantially improve it. Question: config_004 (RNA-only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a single-variable change from config_001—only the RNA encoder shifts from linear PCA to a learned variational autoencoder—so it cleanly isolates the effect of representation quality. Why this is the best next step: (1) It directly tests whether the 48.5% baseline is a representation limitation or a data limitation, which fundamentally shapes all downstream decisions (multiprofile, fusion, encoder choice). (2) If scvi substantially outperforms PCA, we gain a strong prior for using learned encoders in multiprofile and multimodal settings, making later experiments more targeted. If it does not, we learn that the RNA signal is inherently limited under these conditions and can redirect budget toward aggregation or fusion. (3) It avoids the confound of simultaneously changing encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, keeping the comparison interpretable under a tight budget.
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the effect of representation quality by replacing the linear PCA-2000 encoder with a learned scvi_n200 variational autoencoder in the otherwise identical RNA-only, single-profile configuration. The validation accuracy improved from ~48.5% (F1 ~46.4%) to ~52.0% (F1 ~49.8%), a modest ~3.5-point gain that indicates a learned nonlinear encoder captures some additional structure beyond linear PCA, yet the relatively small improvement also suggests the single-profile RNA signal may be partially data-limited rather than purely representation-limited. It remains uncertain whether this encoder advantage would compound in multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion settings, and whether the ~52% level is near the practical ceiling for RNA-only single-profile models or whether further architectural changes could yield substantially larger gains.

selection_reason: Evidence: Three experiments establish that RNA is the dominant modality (~48-52% vs ~21% for image) and that the learned scvi_n200 encoder outperforms PCA-2000 by ~3.5 points in the single-profile setting. However, all experiments so far are single-profile; the effect of multiprofile aggregation is completely untested. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) adds meaningful signal beyond a single profile, and whether the encoder advantage of scvi_n200 compounds or diminishes under aggregation. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) tests the single design decision of adding multiprofile + avgpool on top of the best-known RNA encoder, directly comparable to config_004. If it yields a substantial gain over 52%, aggregation is a key axis to exploit; if the gain is marginal, it tells us the single-profile RNA signal is near its ceiling and we should pivot to testing fusion or alternative encoders. This is the highest-information next step because it resolves the most critical unexplored axis (profile/aggregation) while keeping the encoder at its best-validated setting, and it uses the simpler avgpool before committing to the more complex transformer.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the effect of multiprofile aggregation via avgpool on the RNA-only, scvi_n200 configuration, directly comparable to the single-profile scvi_n200 baseline (llm_summary_003). The validation accuracy rose from ~52.0% to ~65.0% (F1 from ~49.8% to ~62.8%), a substantial ~13-point gain indicating that aggregating multiple profiles adds significant signal beyond a single profile and is a high-leverage axis of improvement, far exceeding the ~3.5-point encoder-quality gain observed earlier. It remains uncertain whether more complex aggregation strategies (e.g., transformer) could push beyond ~65%, whether this gain compounds with cross-modal fusion or alternative encoders, and whether the previously weak image modality might contribute more in a multiprofile context.

selection_reason: Evidence: Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) produced the largest single gain observed (~13 points, 52%→65%), making aggregation the highest-leverage design axis. The scvi_n200 encoder added a modest +3.5 points over PCA, and image-only signal is very weak (~21%). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the aggregation *strategy* (avgpool vs. transformer) matters, or whether ~65% is near the RNA-only ceiling. This experiment (config_006) directly tests transformer aggregation in an otherwise identical setup to config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200), isolating the aggregation architecture as the sole variable. If transformer substantially improves over avgpool, it signals that richer aggregation will be critical in multimodal fusion and justifies prioritizing transformer-based configs later. If it does not, it confirms avgpool is near-optimal, simplifying the search space and letting us focus budget on encoder choice or fusion strategy. This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest evidence (multiprofile is the key lever) while reducing uncertainty on a sub-decision that will gate many future multimodal configurations, all without introducing the additional confounds of a new modality or encoder.
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the aggregation architecture by replacing avgpool with a transformer in the otherwise identical RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~65.3% (F1 ~62.8%) is essentially unchanged from the avgpool result of ~65.0% (F1 ~62.8%), a negligible ~0.3-point difference suggesting that transformer aggregation does not substantially outperform simple average pooling and that ~65% may represent a practical ceiling for RNA-only multiprofile models under this encoder. It remains uncertain whether alternative encoders, the previously weak image modality in a multiprofile context, or cross-modal fusion could push beyond this level, and whether the near-equivalence of aggregation strategies would hold under different data scales or architectural combinations.

selection_reason: Evidence: The image-only single-profile baseline (config_010) yielded only ~20.8% accuracy, far below the RNA-only baselines, but this was tested with a single profile. For RNA, moving from single-profile to multi-profile was the single largest lever discovered (+13 points, config_004→config_005). It is currently unknown whether the image modality's apparent weakness is due to an inherent lack of signal or simply the single-profile limitation. Question tested: config_011 (image-only, multi-profile, ResNet50, avgpool) directly parallels the RNA multi-profile experiment and isolates whether multi-profile aggregation recovers meaningful image signal. Why this is the best next experiment: The result will determine whether any multimodal fusion experiment is worth pursuing. If image multi-profile remains very weak (~20-30%), it strongly suggests the image modality carries little independent signal and budget should be redirected to RNA-only improvements (e.g., scgpt encoder). If it jumps substantially, it validates the image modality and justifies investing in multimodal fusion configs. This single, clean experiment resolves a major branch of the search tree and avoids committing budget to multimodal configurations whose value is currently unestablished.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether multiprofile avgpool aggregation could recover meaningful signal from the image modality, directly paralleling the RNA multiprofile experiment (llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~32.8% (F1 ~28.8%) represents a ~12-point improvement over the image-only single-profile baseline (~20.8%, llm_summary_002), confirming that the single-profile limitation was a contributing factor to the image modality's apparent weakness, yet the image modality remains substantially weaker than the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (~65.0%). This suggests the image modality carries considerably less independent predictive signal than RNA even after multiprofile aggregation, though it remains uncertain whether alternative image encoders, more complex aggregation, or multimodal fusion could extract additional value from the residual image signal, and whether ~32.8% is near the practical ceiling for image-only multiprofile models.

selection_reason: Evidence: The best result so far is ~65.3% (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer; config_006), with avgpool essentially equivalent at ~65.0% (config_005). The image modality alone is weak (~32.8% multiprofile, config_011), but it remains entirely untested whether image adds complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. This is the largest remaining design uncertainty. Question: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends the best RNA-only multiprofile setup by adding the image modality via simple concat fusion, using the same resnet50 encoder for which we already have a single-modality baseline. It isolates the fusion question: does the residual image signal contribute beyond the ~65% RNA-only ceiling? Why this is the best next experiment: it tests the highest-leverage unexplored axis (cross-modal fusion) with the strongest known RNA backbone and the simplest reasonable fusion/aggregation choices, avoiding confounds. If it exceeds 65%, we confirm multimodal fusion is productive and can then optimize fusion strategy (weighted) and image encoder (ViT-L). If it does not, we learn the image modality is not complementary under this setup and can redirect budget toward RNA-only encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt) or alternative image encoders. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the most impactful remaining design decision.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether adding the image modality (ResNet50, avgpool) via simple concat fusion to the strongest RNA-only multiprofile backbone (scvi_n200, avgpool) would push beyond the ~65% RNA-only ceiling. The validation accuracy of ~63.2% (F1 ~60.7%) is slightly below the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool baseline (~65.0%), an initial observation suggesting that the residual image signal does not provide complementary predictive information under this configuration and may introduce mild interference, though the ~1.8-point gap is small and the specific contributor (image content, ResNet50 encoder quality, or the concat mechanism) cannot be isolated from this single experiment. It remains uncertain whether alternative fusion strategies (e.g., weighted or attention-based), stronger image encoders, or different image-branch aggregation could recover or exceed the RNA-only performance, or whether the image modality is fundamentally non-complementary for this task.

selection_reason: The strongest RNA-only multiprofile baseline (scvi_n200, avgpool) achieves ~65.0% accuracy, but adding the image modality via concat fusion (config_030) actually *decreased* performance to ~63.2%. The critical uncertainty is whether this ~1.8-point drop is caused by the concat fusion mechanism (which treats both modalities equally and cannot down-weight a weak signal) or by the image content itself being non-complementary. Config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, keeping all other settings identical to config_030 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This single-variable comparison isolates the fusion strategy: if weighted fusion recovers to ≥65%, it indicates the image carries complementary signal that concat fails to exploit; if it remains below 65%, it strongly suggests the ResNet50-encoded image is fundamentally non-complementary under this setup, saving budget from further image-encoder or aggregation variants. This is the most information-dense next experiment because it directly addresses the key open question (can multimodal beat RNA-only?) with minimal confounding, and the answer will determine whether subsequent budget should go toward stronger image encoders or toward RNA-only encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt).
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the fusion mechanism by replacing concat with weighted fusion in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile configuration (scvi_n200 + ResNet50, avgpool), directly comparable to llm_summary_007. Validation accuracy rose from ~63.2% to ~67.8% (F1 from ~60.7% to ~64.6%), a ~4.6-point gain attributable to the fusion change, and now exceeds the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool baseline (~65.0%, llm_summary_004) by ~2.8 points, indicating that the image modality does carry complementary signal that concat fails to exploit and that weighted fusion effectively down-weights the weaker image contribution. It remains uncertain whether attention-based or learned fusion could push further beyond ~67.8%, whether stronger image encoders or image-specific aggregation could amplify the residual image contribution, and whether this gain is stable across different data splits or task formulations.

selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_031, 67.8% acc) uses weighted fusion to successfully leverage a weak image signal (~2.8 points above RNA-only multiprofile). The image modality remains the weakest component (image-only multiprofile: 32.8% vs RNA-only multiprofile: 65.0%), and we have only tested ResNet50 as the image encoder. Config_037 replaces ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup, isolating the effect of image encoder quality. If ViT-L substantially improves the image branch, the weighted fusion should amplify the complementary signal and push beyond 67.8%; if not, it confirms the image modality is fundamentally data-limited rather than encoder-limited. This is a single-variable change from the current best, making it the most informative and efficient next step: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (weighted fusion works, multiprofile is critical) while reducing uncertainty about whether the residual image contribution can be amplified with a stronger representation.
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the effect of image encoder quality by replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted-fusion configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_008). Validation accuracy rose from ~67.8% to ~70.6% (F1 from ~64.6% to ~66.7%), a ~2.8-point gain attributable to the encoder swap, indicating that the image branch was at least partially encoder-limited and that a stronger visual representation can amplify the complementary signal exploited by weighted fusion. It remains uncertain whether further encoder improvements, alternative image-branch aggregation, or different fusion mechanisms could push beyond ~70.6%, and whether the residual image contribution is now approaching a data-limited ceiling.

selection_reason: The current best (config_037, 70.6%) uses scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, but scgpt has not been tested in any configuration. Since RNA is the dominant signal source (RNA-only multiprofile achieves ~65% vs. image-only ~33%), the RNA encoder choice is a high-leverage axis. Config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) directly parallels config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, 65.0%), changing only the RNA encoder. This cleanly isolates whether scgpt captures more predictive structure than scvi_n200. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, the gain could compound with multiprofile aggregation, weighted fusion, and ViT-L in a follow-up multimodal experiment. If it does not, an entire branch of the search space (all scgpt configurations) is effectively ruled out, saving future budget for other axes. This is preferred over testing scgpt directly in the full multimodal setting (e.g., config_049) because the simpler RNA-only comparison provides cleaner attribution, and over testing transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting (config_039) because transformer≈avgpool is already well-established from the RNA-only evidence.
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the RNA encoder by substituting scgpt for scvi_n200 in the otherwise identical RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~53.0% (F1 ~51.5%) is approximately 12 points below the scvi_n200 result (~65.0%, F1 ~62.8%), a substantial gap cleanly attributable to the encoder swap, indicating that scgpt captures considerably less predictive structure than scvi_n200 for this task. This result suggests the scgpt branch of the search space is unlikely to be competitive and can be deprioritized, though it remains uncertain whether scgpt might behave differently under multimodal fusion, alternative aggregation strategies, or different data scales.

selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence for any design choice. The most critical uncertainty is the absolute performance floor: how well does the simplest possible configuration (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) perform? Establishing this baseline is essential before interpreting whether more complex encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image modalities, or multimodal fusion actually add value. Config_001 is the minimal configuration in the design space—no image encoder, no aggregation, no fusion—making it the cleanest reference point. All subsequent experiments can be understood as adding one or more design choices on top of this floor, which allows us to isolate the marginal contribution of each decision. Under a limited budget, spending one experiment on the simplest baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment by anchoring the entire comparison grid.
experiment_summary: This experiment established the performance floor for the multimodal cellular profiling study using the minimal RNA-only configuration (single profile, PCA-2000 encoder, no image encoder, no aggregation, no fusion), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.485 and F1 of 0.464. As the first completed experiment, this result serves as a baseline reference point; no comparative evidence yet exists to attribute this performance to any specific design choice. It remains uncertain whether more complex RNA encoders (e.g., scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, image modalities, or multimodal fusion can meaningfully improve upon this ~0.485 accuracy floor.

selection_reason: Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), establishing a low baseline. The largest source of uncertainty is whether the RNA representation itself is the bottleneck—PCA-2000 is a linear projection, while scvi_n200 is a learned nonlinear latent representation specifically designed for single-cell data. Question: Does replacing the linear PCA encoder with the learned scvi encoder (holding profile setting, modality, aggregation, and fusion all identical to the baseline) meaningfully improve validation accuracy? Why this is the best next experiment: It changes exactly one design variable (RNA encoder) relative to the established baseline, making the comparison clean and interpretable. If scvi substantially outperforms PCA, it confirms that representation quality is a primary lever and justifies further investment in encoder choice and downstream multimodal designs built on scvi. If it does not, it signals that the RNA signal alone is limited, redirecting budget toward image or multimodal experiments. Under a tight budget, isolating the encoder effect before layering on multiprofile aggregation or image fusion avoids confounding multiple changes and yields the highest information-per-experiment.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced the PCA-2000 linear encoder with the learned scvi_n200 nonlinear encoder while holding all other design variables constant (single profile, RNA-only, no aggregation, no fusion), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.520 and F1 of 0.498 versus the PCA baseline of 0.485 and 0.464. Because exactly one variable (the RNA encoder) was changed, the ~3.5-point accuracy gain is cleanly attributable to the encoder choice, indicating that nonlinear learned representations provide a modest but real improvement over linear projection in the RNA-only setting. However, absolute performance remains moderate, leaving it uncertain whether the RNA signal itself is the primary bottleneck and whether the scvi encoder's advantage will persist when combined with multiprofile aggregation or image-based multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have two RNA-only single-profile experiments showing that a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200, 0.520 acc) modestly beats a linear one (PCA-2000, 0.485 acc). However, the image modality is entirely unexplored—we have zero data on whether image features carry independent predictive signal. This is the largest source of uncertainty in the design space, as it determines whether the 36 multimodal configurations (configs 016-051) are worth pursuing at all. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single profile, ResNet-50) establishes the performance floor for the image modality in direct analogy to how config_001 established the RNA floor. It isolates the image encoder's contribution with no confounding from RNA, aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Before investing limited budget in complex multimodal fusion or multiprofile aggregation, we need to know whether the image signal is strong enough to be worth combining. If image-only performs competitively (≥0.50), multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction; if it is weak (<0.45), we should focus remaining budget on RNA improvements (multiprofile, scgpt encoder). This single experiment gates the entire multimodal branch of the search and is the highest-information, lowest-confounding next step.
experiment_summary: This experiment established the performance floor for the image modality using a single-profile, image-only configuration with a ResNet-50 encoder (no RNA, no aggregation, no fusion), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.208 and F1 of 0.172. This is substantially below the RNA-only baselines (0.485 for PCA-2000, 0.520 for scvi_n200), suggesting that image features carry very weak independent predictive signal for this classification task. It remains uncertain whether image features could still contribute meaningfully when fused with RNA representations, whether alternative image encoders or preprocessing might recover more signal, or whether the low performance reflects a fundamental limitation of the image modality for this task.

selection_reason: Evidence: scvi_n200 outperforms PCA-2000 by ~3.5 points in the single-profile RNA-only setting (0.520 vs 0.485), establishing scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder so far. Image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), suggesting the RNA pipeline should be optimized before adding a multimodal component. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether multiprofile aggregation adds meaningful signal on top of the scvi_n200 encoder, or whether the single-profile representation already captures the relevant information. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) tests exactly that question with the simplest aggregation strategy, changing only the profile/aggregation axis from the best RNA-only result (config_004). If avgpool yields a clear gain, it justifies testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not, it suggests multiprofile is not a productive direction and budget should shift to encoder comparison (scgpt) or multimodal fusion. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice because it resolves a key design axis (profile aggregation) on the strongest known RNA backbone before committing budget to more complex multimodal or aggregation variants.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) on the scvi_n200 RNA encoder, changing only the profile/aggregation axis from the best prior RNA-only result (single-profile scvi_n200, 0.520 acc / 0.498 F1), and achieved a validation accuracy of 0.650 and F1 of 0.628. Because the encoder and modality were held constant, the ~13-point accuracy gain is cleanly attributable to the multiprofile + avgpool aggregation, confirming that combining multiple profiles adds substantial predictive signal beyond what the single-profile scvi_n200 representation captures. It remains uncertain whether more expressive aggregation strategies (e.g., transformer) could yield further gains, whether this multiprofile advantage persists once an image modality is introduced, and how much additional headroom exists above the current ~0.65 accuracy.

selection_reason: The strongest finding so far is that multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) on scvi_n200 RNA yielded a ~13-point accuracy gain (0.520→0.650, config_005), making aggregation the most impactful design axis identified. The key uncertainty is whether avgpool is near-optimal or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation can extract additional signal from the multi-profile representations. config_006 changes exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool→transformer) relative to the current best (config_005), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it reveals further headroom in the aggregation axis and justifies exploring transformer in multimodal settings later; if it does not, it confirms avgpool is sufficient and redirects the budget toward other axes (encoder choice via scgpt, or the multimodal fusion question). This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the largest observed effect with a minimal, interpretable change, avoiding the confound of simultaneously introducing a weak image modality (config_010 showed image alone is only 0.208) before fully characterizing the RNA-side design space.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced avgpool with transformer aggregation in the multiprofile scvi_n200 RNA-only setting (the single-variable change from the current best, config_005), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.653 and F1 of 0.628 versus 0.650 and 0.628 for avgpool. The negligible ~0.3-point accuracy difference suggests that a more expressive transformer aggregation provides no meaningful improvement over simple average pooling for combining multi-profile scvi_n200 representations, indicating the aggregation axis is near its practical ceiling under the current encoder. It remains uncertain whether this null result generalizes to other encoders (e.g., scgpt) or whether the remaining headroom lies in the encoder-choice axis or the multimodal fusion question, which are the next unexplored design axes.

selection_reason: Evidence: The current best (config_005/006, ~0.65 acc) uses scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool. We've cleanly isolated that multiprofile aggregation contributes +13pp over single-profile and that transformer vs avgpool is negligible. The one major RNA encoder axis still untested is scgpt. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting, i.e., can we push beyond the ~0.65 ceiling by swapping the encoder while holding the proven-best profile/aggregation settings constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder) relative to config_005, giving a clean encoder comparison in the highest-performing regime. It avoids the very-weak image modality (0.208 acc) where fusion gains are unlikely, and it avoids redundant aggregation variants (transformer ≈ avgpool). If scgpt matches or beats scvi, it informs which encoder to pair with multimodal fusion later; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the best encoder and redirects budget toward the fusion axis.
experiment_summary: This experiment swapped the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding the multiprofile + avgpool RNA-only configuration constant (the single-variable change from the current best, config_004), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.530 and F1 of 0.515 versus 0.650 and 0.628 for scvi_n200 in the identical multiprofile avgpool setting. Because only the encoder was changed, the ~12-point accuracy drop is cleanly attributable to the encoder choice, indicating that scvi_n200 is the substantially superior RNA encoder for this classification task and that the ~0.65 accuracy ceiling observed with scvi_n200 is not an artifact of the encoder. It remains uncertain whether scgpt could perform differently under alternative aggregation strategies or in a multimodal fusion context, and whether the remaining headroom above 0.65 lies in the fusion axis or in further tuning of the scvi_n200 pipeline.

selection_reason: The RNA-only pipeline is now well-characterized: scvi_n200 is the clear best encoder (config_004 vs 001, config_008), multiprofile+avgpool gives the largest single gain (+13pp, config_005), and transformer aggregation adds nothing over avgpool (config_006). The current best is ~0.65 accuracy. The biggest remaining uncertainty is the multimodal fusion axis, which is completely untested. Image alone (ResNet50, config_010) is very weak (0.208), so it is genuinely uncertain whether image features add complementary signal or merely noise when fused with the strong RNA representation. Config_030 takes the proven best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with the simplest possible fusion (concat), changing only the modality/fusion axis. This directly answers whether the image modality contributes any incremental value above the 0.65 RNA-only ceiling. If concat helps, weighted fusion and ViT encoders become natural follow-ups; if it does not, we avoid wasting budget on the full 24-config multimodal grid. This is the highest-information experiment under the remaining budget because it resolves the single largest open design question with a minimal, interpretable change.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the first multimodal configuration by adding ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion to the proven best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.632 and F1 of 0.607. This is slightly below the RNA-only best (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1), indicating that the addition of ResNet50 image features via concat fusion does not provide incremental predictive value over the strong RNA representation and may introduce a small amount of noise. It remains uncertain whether alternative fusion strategies (e.g., weighted or attention-based) or different image encoders (e.g., ViT) could extract complementary signal from the image modality, or whether the image features are fundamentally uninformative for this classification task.

selection_reason: Evidence: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.632 acc, slightly below the RNA-only best (0.650/0.653), suggesting concat fusion of weak image features introduces noise. However, it remains unclear whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative or whether the simple concat fusion is the bottleneck. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted, holding all other variables constant (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50). This isolates the fusion axis. If weighted fusion recovers performance toward or above 0.650, it indicates the image carries complementary signal that needs proper weighting, justifying further investment in image encoders (e.g., ViT-L). If it does not help, it strongly suggests ResNet50 image features are uninformative for this task, allowing us to deprioritize the image modality and focus budget on other axes. This is the most informative single-variable experiment because it directly resolves the key uncertainty about whether the image modality is worth pursuing, and the result will guide all subsequent multimodal decisions.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted in the multimodal setting (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.678 and F1 of 0.646, a ~4.6-point improvement over the identical pipeline with concat fusion (0.632 acc / 0.607 F1) and ~2.8 points above the RNA-only best (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Because the single-variable change isolates the fusion axis, the gain is attributable to weighted fusion, indicating that ResNet50 image features carry complementary predictive signal that simple concatenation was suppressing and that proper modality weighting is necessary to unlock it. This resolves the key uncertainty from the prior concat experiment: the image modality is worth pursuing, justifying further investment in stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and alternative fusion strategies. It remains uncertain whether the weighted-fusion advantage generalizes to other image encoders, whether additional headroom exists above 0.678, and whether more sophisticated fusion mechanisms (e.g., attention-based) could yield further gains.

selection_reason: The current best (config_031: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; 0.678 acc) shows that image features do carry complementary signal when properly fused, but ResNet50's standalone performance was very weak (0.208). The key remaining uncertainty is whether a stronger, more expressive image encoder (ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L) can extract meaningfully more complementary visual signal beyond what ResNet50 captures. Config_037 changes exactly one variable (image encoder: resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while holding the proven optimal settings constant (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), making the result cleanly attributable to encoder quality. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) the fusion axis is confirmed productive (weighted >> concat), so a better image representation should yield larger gains; (2) the aggregation axis is near-ceiling (avgpool ≈ transformer), so no need to revisit it; (3) the RNA encoder is settled (scvi_n200 >> scgpt); and (4) this directly tests whether further investment in the image modality is justified or whether the ~0.678 level is near the practical ceiling for this task.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced the ResNet50 image encoder with an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L (imagenet_vit_l) while holding all other settings constant (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted fusion), achieving a validation accuracy of 0.706 and F1 of 0.667, a ~2.8-point accuracy improvement over the identical pipeline with ResNet50 (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Because only the image encoder was changed, the gain is cleanly attributable to the encoder, confirming that a stronger, more expressive visual representation extracts meaningfully more complementary signal beyond what ResNet50 captures and further justifying continued investment in the image modality. It remains uncertain whether the ~0.706 accuracy approaches a practical ceiling for this task, whether alternative fusion strategies (e.g., attention-based) could yield further gains, or whether even stronger image encoders would continue to produce incremental improvements.

selection_reason: The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1. The aggregation axis showed a near-null result in the RNA-only setting (avgpool 0.650 vs transformer 0.653, ~0.3 pts), but that null was measured without an image modality. In the multimodal pipeline, the aggregated RNA representation is subsequently fused with image features via weighted fusion, so the interaction between aggregation strategy and downstream fusion may differ. Config_039 is a single-variable change from config_037 (avgpool → transformer, all else identical), cleanly isolating whether transformer aggregation extracts additional profile-level structure that benefits the weighted fusion step. If it yields a meaningful gain, it identifies a new lever above 0.706; if it is again null, it confirms the aggregation axis is saturated in the multimodal context and redirects remaining budget toward other unexplored axes. This is the most efficient exploitation of the current best direction while resolving the last untested design variable in the proven pipeline.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced avgpool with transformer aggregation in the current best multimodal pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion), a single-variable change from config_037, achieving a validation accuracy of 0.725 and F1 of 0.685, a ~1.9-point accuracy and ~1.8-point F1 improvement over the avgpool baseline (0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). This contrasts with the near-null result (~0.3 pts) observed for the same aggregation swap in the RNA-only setting, suggesting that transformer aggregation extracts profile-level structure that is specifically beneficial when the RNA representation is subsequently fused with image features via weighted fusion, though the mechanism behind this interaction remains unverified. It is uncertain whether the ~1.9-point gain is robust across random seeds, whether further headroom exists above 0.725 from other unexplored axes (e.g., attention-based fusion, alternative encoder combinations), and whether the aggregation–fusion interaction generalizes beyond the current configuration.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which design choices (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion) matter or whether the task is solvable at all. The largest uncertainty is whether a basic single-modality model can achieve meaningful performance, which is the necessary reference point for all subsequent comparisons. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration in the design space—no image processing, no learned RNA encoder, no multi-profile aggregation, no fusion. It establishes the performance floor and confirms the pipeline runs correctly. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first experiment should anchor the search. By establishing the simplest baseline, every future experiment (e.g., swapping in scvi/scgpt encoders, adding multiprofile aggregation, adding image modality, or testing fusion strategies) can be interpreted as a controlled increment over this reference. Choosing a more complex configuration first would conflate multiple design decisions and make it impossible to attribute performance gains to specific choices. config_001 maximizes information per experiment by providing the cleanest possible comparison anchor.
experiment_summary: This first experiment tested the minimal baseline configuration: RNA-only modality, single profile, PCA (2000 components) as the RNA encoder, with no image processing, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy of 0.485 (F1 0.464) establishes a reference performance floor, indicating that a simple dimensionality-reduction pipeline on RNA alone yields modest but non-trivial classification performance. Because no other configurations have been evaluated, it remains uncertain whether this level of accuracy reflects inherent task difficulty, a limitation of the PCA encoder, or the absence of complementary modalities, learned encoders, and aggregation strategies.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one data point (config_001: RNA-only, single profile, PCA → acc 0.485). The most critical unknown is whether the image modality carries complementary signal that can improve classification beyond RNA alone. Without this, we cannot determine whether the large multimodal portion of the search space (configs 016–051) is worth exploring. 2) What this tests: config_016 keeps the RNA pipeline identical to config_001 (PCA n2000, single profile) and adds only the image modality via ResNet-50 with a simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding image information as the sole conceptual change, allowing a direct apples-to-apples comparison against the RNA-only baseline. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, the highest-impact question is 'does image help at all?' A positive result validates the multimodal direction and justifies subsequent experiments on image encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion type. A null or negative result would redirect effort toward improving the RNA encoder or profile/aggregation strategy, saving many experiments on multimodal variants that would likely underperform. It is the minimal, single-conceptual-change extension of the baseline, satisfying the principle of isolating one design decision.
experiment_summary: This experiment added an image modality (ResNet-50 encoder, concat fusion) to the RNA-only baseline (PCA n2000, single profile), keeping the RNA pipeline identical to config_001, to test whether image features provide complementary classification signal. The multimodal configuration achieved a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1 0.510), a clear increase over the RNA-only baseline of 0.485 (F1 0.464), suggesting that the image modality contributes useful information beyond RNA alone. It remains uncertain whether this gain is specific to the ResNet-50 encoder and concat fusion choices, whether alternative fusion or aggregation strategies could further improve performance, and whether the observed improvement is stable under repeated runs.

selection_reason: Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA, single) achieved 0.485 acc / 0.464 F1, while config_016 (multimodal, PCA + ResNet50, concat, single) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a ~4.2% accuracy gain. However, we cannot yet decompose whether this gain comes from the image modality's independent predictive strength or from genuine cross-modal complementarity. Question: config_010 (image-only, single profile, ResNet50) establishes the image-only baseline using the exact same image encoder and profile setting as config_016, isolating the image modality's standalone contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: Without this baseline, we cannot calibrate how much of the multimodal gain is attributable to the image alone versus the fusion interaction, which is critical for deciding whether to invest further in fusion strategies, alternative encoders, or aggregation. It is a single-variable change (removing RNA) from config_016, making the comparison clean and informative. This foundational measurement will guide whether subsequent experiments should focus on improving fusion (config_017), adding multiprofile aggregation (config_018), or switching encoders.
experiment_summary: This image-only experiment (ResNet-50, single profile, no RNA) was designed to isolate the image modality's standalone contribution by removing RNA from the multimodal config_016. The validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172) is dramatically below both the RNA-only baseline (0.485) and the multimodal configuration (0.527), indicating that the image modality provides very weak standalone predictive signal in this setup and that the ~4.2% multimodal gain over RNA-only is unlikely to be attributable to the image's independent strength. It remains uncertain whether the multimodal improvement reflects genuine cross-modal complementarity, a specific property of the concat fusion with PCA features, or some other factor, and whether the poor image-only performance stems from a ResNet-50 limitation on this imaging data, the absence of aggregation, or inherent task difficulty for the image modality alone.

selection_reason: Evidence: RNA (PCA n2000) is the dominant modality (0.485 acc) while image alone is very weak (0.208 acc). The multimodal gain (+4.2%) is modest and may be limited by the quality of the RNA representation. PCA is a linear method; whether a learned encoder (scvi_n200) captures nonlinear gene-expression structure that PCA misses is the single most important unresolved question, because it affects every downstream configuration (RNA-only, multimodal, multiprofile). Question: Does replacing PCA with a learned scvi encoder improve classification in the simplest RNA-only, single-profile setting? This is a clean single-variable change from config_001 (only the RNA encoder differs). Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It isolates the RNA-encoder effect without confounding from fusion, aggregation, or modality changes. (2) The result directly gates many future experiments—if scvi substantially outperforms PCA, we pivot to scvi-based multimodal configs; if it does not, PCA is sufficient and we redirect budget toward multiprofile/aggregation or fusion strategy. (3) Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental representation question before adding complexity (multiprofile, weighted fusion, ViT-L) avoids wasting experiments on configurations built on a suboptimal encoder assumption.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced the PCA (n2000) RNA encoder with a learned scVI encoder (n200) in the RNA-only, single-profile setting, constituting a single-variable change from the baseline (llm_summary_001). The scVI configuration achieved a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1 0.498), a ~3.5% improvement over the PCA baseline (0.485, F1 0.464), suggesting that a learned nonlinear encoder captures gene-expression structure beyond what linear PCA provides. However, because the encoder dimensionality also changed (200 vs. 2000), it remains uncertain whether the gain is attributable to the learned representation, the reduced dimensionality, or both, and whether this improvement will transfer to multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

selection_reason: Evidence: config_004 showed scVI (n200) improves RNA-only accuracy from 0.485 (PCA) to 0.520, and config_016 showed adding ResNet50 image with concat fusion to PCA RNA yields 0.527. However, we have no evidence on whether the scVI encoder gain is additive with the multimodal gain or whether it interacts with the image modality. Question: config_028 (multimodal, single profile, scVI n200, ResNet50, concat) is a single-variable change from config_016 (PCA→scVI), directly testing whether the learned-encoder improvement transfers to the multimodal setting. If it exceeds 0.527, the encoder and modality gains are independent and we should build on scVI going forward; if it plateaus near 0.520, the image contribution was specific to PCA's high-dimensional features; if it drops below 0.527, scVI's lower dimensionality may be incompatible with the current fusion. This is the highest-information next step because it resolves the most consequential open question—whether to anchor future multiprofile/fusion experiments on scVI or PCA—while changing only one variable relative to the current best configuration.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced the PCA (n2000) RNA encoder with a learned scVI encoder (n200) in the multimodal, single-profile, ResNet-50, concat-fusion setting, constituting a single-variable change from llm_summary_002. The configuration achieved a validation accuracy of 0.536 (F1 0.516), exceeding both the PCA-based multimodal baseline (0.527, F1 0.510) and the RNA-only scVI result (0.520, F1 0.498), suggesting that the scVI encoder gain is at least partially additive with the multimodal image contribution. It remains uncertain whether the modest ~0.9% improvement over the PCA multimodal configuration is stable across runs, whether the gain is driven by the learned representation or the reduced dimensionality (200 vs. 2000), and whether this advantage persists under alternative fusion strategies or multiprofile settings.

selection_reason: All five completed experiments are singleprofile; the multiprofile + aggregation axis is entirely unexplored and represents the largest remaining source of uncertainty. config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-conceptual-change from config_004 (RNA-only, singleprofile, scVI_n200): it tests whether aggregating multiple profiles (via average pooling) captures complementary per-profile signal that a single profile discards, while keeping the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (scVI) fixed to isolate the profile/aggregation effect from image or fusion confounds. If multiprofile + avgpool yields a meaningful gain over config_004's 0.520, it strongly motivates investing subsequent budget in multiprofile multimodal configurations (e.g., config_030/032); if it does not, we can deprioritize that entire branch and focus on encoder or image improvements. This is the highest-information-value experiment under the limited budget because it resolves a binary design question that gates many downstream configurations, and it does so with the minimal number of changed variables.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether aggregating multiple profiles via average pooling (multiprofile + avgpool) in the RNA-only, scVI_n200 setting captures complementary per-profile signal beyond a single profile, constituting a single conceptual change from llm_summary_004 (RNA-only, singleprofile, scVI_n200, no aggregation). The configuration achieved a validation accuracy of 0.650 (F1 0.628), a substantial ~13% improvement over the singleprofile scVI baseline (0.520, F1 0.498), indicating that multiprofile aggregation captures meaningful complementary signal that a single profile discards. It remains uncertain whether this gain is specific to average pooling versus other aggregation strategies, whether the improvement is stable across repeated runs, and whether the advantage transfers to multimodal or alternative-fusion configurations.

selection_reason: The strongest finding so far is the ~13% accuracy jump from adding multiprofile+avgpool to the RNA-only scVI setting (config_005: 0.650 vs. config_004: 0.520). The second strongest finding is that multimodal concat fusion with ResNet-50 adds a modest but consistent gain over RNA-only (config_028: 0.536 vs. config_004: 0.520). The critical open question is whether these two gains are additive: does the multiprofile aggregation benefit transfer to the multimodal setting? config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the direct logical extension of both config_005 (adding the validated image modality) and config_028 (adding multiprofile+avgpool), testing one conceptual question from each parent. If the gains are additive, this could yield a configuration well above 0.65, establishing a new strong baseline. If they are not additive, we learn an important interaction constraint that would redirect subsequent experiments toward optimizing within the multiprofile RNA-only space rather than pursuing multimodal combinations. Under a limited budget, exploiting the single largest observed effect (multiprofile) in the most promising direction (multimodal, already validated) is the highest-information next step.
experiment_summary: This experiment directly combined multiprofile+avgpool aggregation with multimodal (ResNet-50, concat) fusion under scVI_n200 to test whether the previously observed multiprofile gain (~13% over singleprofile RNA-only) and the multimodal gain (~1.6% over RNA-only) are additive. The validation accuracy of 0.632 (F1 0.607) falls below the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.650, F1 0.628) and well below the simple additive prediction (~0.666), indicating the two gains are not additive; the multimodal configuration with multiprofile aggregation underperforms the RNA-only multiprofile baseline by ~1.9%. The multiprofile benefit is still present in the multimodal setting (0.632 vs. 0.536 for singleprofile multimodal scVI), but adding the image modality on top of multiprofile+avgpool does not yield the expected additional gain. It remains uncertain whether the slight underperformance relative to RNA-only multiprofile reflects noise introduced by the image features, an interaction between concat fusion and avgpool, or other factors, and whether alternative fusion or aggregation strategies could restore or exceed the RNA-only multiprofile performance.

selection_reason: The strongest result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy, and the critical open question is whether the aggregation strategy is optimal. The multimodal multiprofile config (config_030) underperformed the RNA-only multiprofile baseline, suggesting that how profiles are aggregated may interact with downstream fusion. Config_006 is a single-variable change from the best configuration (avgpool → transformer aggregation), directly testing whether a learned, attention-based aggregation captures inter-profile relationships that simple averaging discards. If transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool, it establishes a superior aggregation strategy to carry into multimodal experiments and potentially resolves the config_030 underperformance. If it does not, it confirms avgpool as the right aggregation and redirects effort toward fusion or encoder choices. This is the highest-information single experiment available: it isolates one design axis, builds on the current best result, and its outcome constrains the design of all subsequent multimodal multiprofile experiments.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced average pooling with transformer (attention-based) aggregation in the RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI_n200 setting, constituting a single-variable change from llm_summary_006 to test whether learned inter-profile attention captures signal that simple averaging discards. The validation accuracy of 0.653 (F1 0.628) is essentially equivalent to the avgpool result (0.650, F1 0.628), with only a ~0.3% accuracy difference, suggesting that the aggregation strategy is not a major performance differentiator in the RNA-only multiprofile setting and that both strategies capture the multiprofile gain comparably. It remains uncertain whether the marginal difference reflects a genuine (if small) advantage of transformer aggregation or run-to-run variability, and whether transformer aggregation might interact differently with multimodal fusion, which was the original motivation for testing it given the underperformance of the multimodal multiprofile configuration (llm_summary_007).

selection_reason: Evidence: Multiprofile aggregation is the dominant performance lever (~13% gain over singleprofile), and the current best configurations (config_005/006) use scVI_n200 in the RNA-only multiprofile setting (~0.650-0.653). We have tested PCA and scVI as RNA encoders but have never evaluated scGPT, leaving a critical gap in the encoder landscape. Question: config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) is a clean single-variable swap from config_005 (scVI→scGPT), directly testing whether a different learned encoder captures complementary gene-expression structure that scVI misses in the highest-impact setting. Why best next: Under a limited budget, resolving whether encoder choice beyond scVI matters in the multiprofile regime is the highest-information experiment—if scGPT substantially outperforms scVI, it redefines the search ceiling and justifies further encoder exploration; if it is comparable, it confirms scVI is near-optimal and redirects effort toward fusion/multimodal questions. This avoids the risk of testing a second variable (e.g., fusion strategy) while the encoder dimension remains unexplored in the setting that produces the best results.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced the scVI_n200 RNA encoder with scGPT in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting (a single-variable swap from llm_summary_006), to test whether a different learned encoder captures complementary gene-expression structure in the highest-impact configuration. The validation accuracy of 0.530 (F1 0.515) is substantially below the scVI multiprofile result (0.650, F1 0.628) and only marginally above the singleprofile scVI baseline (0.520, F1 0.498), indicating that the ~13% multiprofile aggregation gain observed with scVI is largely absent when using scGPT. It remains uncertain whether this gap reflects a fundamental limitation of scGPT's learned representation for this task, a dimensionality or hyperparameter mismatch, or run-to-run variability, and whether scGPT might perform differently under alternative aggregation strategies or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: The most important open question is why adding the image modality in the multiprofile setting hurts performance (config_030: 0.632 vs. config_005/006: 0.650/0.653), despite helping in the singleprofile setting (config_028: 0.536 vs. config_004: 0.520). Since image-only performance is very weak (0.208), the image features likely introduce noise that concat fusion passes through undiluted. Config_031 is a single-variable change from config_030 (concat → weighted fusion), directly testing whether learned fusion weights can downweight the noisy image signal and restore/exceed the RNA-only multiprofile baseline. This is the most efficient next experiment: if weighted fusion recovers performance, it identifies fusion as the bottleneck and opens a path to a superior multimodal configuration; if it does not, it confirms the image modality is fundamentally incompatible with strong RNA multiprofile signal, saving future budget from further multimodal-multiprofile exploration. No other single experiment resolves this key design uncertainty as cleanly.
experiment_summary: This experiment replaced concat fusion with weighted fusion in the multimodal, multiprofile, scVI_n200, ResNet-50, avgpool setting (a single-variable change from llm_summary_007) to test whether learned fusion weights can downweight the weak image signal (image-only accuracy: 0.208) and address the underperformance observed with concat fusion. The validation accuracy of 0.678 (F1 0.646) exceeds the concat-fusion counterpart (0.632, F1 0.607) by ~4.6% and surpasses the RNA-only multiprofile baselines (0.650–0.653), indicating that weighted fusion allows the image modality to contribute positively on top of multiprofile RNA signal rather than degrading it; this is the highest validation accuracy observed in the study to date. It remains uncertain whether this gain is stable across repeated runs, whether alternative fusion or aggregation strategies could yield further improvements, and whether the weighted-fusion advantage is specific to the scVI_n200 encoder or generalizes across other encoder choices.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about the performance landscape. The most fundamental unknown is the baseline performance of the simplest possible model. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal RNA-only configuration, using a simple linear PCA projection as the encoder. It establishes the performance floor for RNA-based classification and tells us how much predictive signal is present in the raw transcriptomic data without any learned or nonlinear representation. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Starting from the simplest configuration provides a clean reference point against which every subsequent design choice (better RNA encoders like scvi/scgpt, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be measured. If this baseline is already strong, it tells us the RNA signal is sufficient and we should focus on marginal gains; if it is weak, it motivates exploring richer encoders or additional modalities. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the starting point of the entire search and is the natural anchor for all future comparisons.
experiment_summary: This experiment established the search baseline by testing the simplest RNA-only configuration (single profile, PCA-2000 encoder, no image, no fusion), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.485 with a supporting F1 of 0.464. As the first completed experiment, this result serves as the performance floor for RNA-based classification and provides the reference point against which all subsequent design choices (richer RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) will be measured. It remains uncertain whether this accuracy is near the ceiling achievable with RNA data alone or whether substantially richer representations or additional modalities could produce meaningful gains.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only completed experiment (config_001, RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile) yields 0.485 accuracy, establishing a floor but leaving the most fundamental question unanswered: does the image modality carry useful signal for this task at all? Without knowing this, the search space splits into two very different strategies (RNA-focused vs. multimodal), and ~30 of the 51 configurations become irrelevant if image is uninformative. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) isolates the modality question with the simplest possible image pipeline, directly comparable in structural complexity to config_001. It tells us whether image features alone can approach, match, or exceed the RNA-only baseline, which determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and which modality should be the anchor. 3) Why best use of budget: With only one data point, the highest-value experiment is the one that most sharply reduces uncertainty about a top-level design axis. The modality question is more fundamental than encoder choice or profile aggregation—its answer will prune or prioritize large swaths of the remaining search space, making every subsequent experiment more targeted. Testing a richer RNA encoder (e.g., scvi) or multiprofile aggregation would be informative but less decisive, since those improvements are only relevant within the RNA branch and do not resolve whether the image channel should be included at all.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the image-only modality (single profile, ResNet50 encoder, no fusion) to isolate whether image features carry useful signal for the task, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), substantially below the RNA-only baseline of 0.485 (F1 0.464). The result suggests that, under this simple pipeline, image features alone provide considerably less discriminative signal than RNA features, positioning RNA as the more promising anchor modality for subsequent experiments. It remains uncertain whether a different image encoder, alternative preprocessing, or multimodal fusion with RNA could recover meaningful signal from the image channel, so the image modality is not yet definitively ruled out.

selection_reason: With only two completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether the PCA-2000 encoder is near the RNA ceiling or whether a learned representation can substantially improve RNA-based classification. Config_004 (scvi_n200, single profile, RNA-only) changes exactly one factor from the config_001 baseline—the RNA encoder—while holding profile setting, modality, and fusion constant. This cleanly isolates the encoder effect. If scvi_n200 meaningfully outperforms PCA-2000 (0.485), it indicates the representation is a bottleneck and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and richer multimodal builds. If it performs similarly, it suggests PCA already captures most useful linear structure, redirecting effort toward multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion. Given the sparse evidence, this single-variable comparison is the highest-information-per-experiment choice before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.
experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the RNA encoder effect by replacing PCA-2000 with scvi_n200 while holding all other settings (RNA-only, single profile, no fusion) constant relative to the llm_summary_001 baseline, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1 0.498) versus 0.485 (F1 0.464) for PCA-2000. Because only the encoder changed, this single-variable comparison indicates that a learned non-linear representation captures structure that PCA-2000 misses, but the ~3.5-point gain is moderate rather than transformative, suggesting the RNA representation is a contributing but not dominant bottleneck. It remains uncertain whether further encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt) would yield larger gains, whether the improvement plateaus within the RNA-only regime, or whether multiprofile aggregation and multimodal fusion (with the image modality at 0.208 accuracy in llm_summary_002) could unlock substantially higher performance.

selection_reason: Evidence: RNA-only single-profile with scvi_n200 achieves 0.520 accuracy (vs 0.485 for PCA-2000), confirming RNA as the dominant modality and scvi_n200 as the current best encoder. Image-only is weak (0.208). The multiprofile axis is completely unexplored—zero experiments have tested whether aggregating multiple profiles per cell adds signal. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the effect of the multiprofile+aggregation design decision while holding the encoder at the currently best performer (scvi_n200). avgpool is the simplest aggregation, making this a clean first test of whether multiprofile helps at all. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it opens a completely new axis with no prior information, which is more informative than a third encoder comparison (scgpt) where the PCA→scvi gain was already modest (~3.5 pts), suggesting we may be near the single-profile RNA ceiling; (2) if multiprofile+avgpool yields a meaningful gain, it justifies testing transformer aggregation (config_006) and multiprofile variants of other encoders; if it does not help, we can deprioritize the entire multiprofile branch and save budget; (3) it uses the best-known encoder, so any gain or loss is attributable to the profile/aggregation decision rather than confounded by a weaker representation.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the effect of multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) by switching from single-profile to multiprofile while holding the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and all other settings constant relative to llm_summary_003, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.650 (F1 0.628) versus 0.520 (F1 0.498) for the single-profile configuration. Because only the profile/aggregation design changed, this clean single-variable comparison indicates that aggregating multiple profiles per cell with a simple average pool captures substantially more discriminative signal than a single profile—a ~13-point gain far exceeding the ~3.5-point encoder improvement observed earlier. It remains uncertain whether a more sophisticated aggregation strategy (e.g., transformer-based) could push accuracy further, whether the multiprofile gain generalizes to other RNA encoders, or whether combining multiprofile aggregation with the image modality or fusion could yield additional improvements.

selection_reason: The strongest result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy, showing that multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever (~13-point gain over single profile). The key remaining uncertainty within this promising regime is whether the aggregation strategy itself can be improved: does a transformer-based aggregation capture inter-profile relationships that a simple average pool misses? config_006 is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (only aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer), directly isolating the aggregation effect. This is the best use of the next experiment because: (1) it exploits the strongest evidence by testing a logical extension of the best configuration, (2) it reduces uncertainty about a design choice that will propagate into all future multimodal experiments, and (3) the answer—whether transformer helps, hurts, or is neutral—will determine whether to invest further in aggregation complexity or pivot to encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal fusion. No other single experiment provides as much information per trial at this stage.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested transformer-based aggregation in the multiprofile RNA-only setting (scvi_n200 encoder) as a single-variable comparison against the avgpool configuration (llm_summary_004), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.653 (F1 0.628) versus 0.650 (F1 0.628) for avgpool. The ~0.3-point accuracy gain and near-identical F1 suggest that, under this configuration, transformer aggregation captures at most a marginal improvement over simple average pooling, indicating that the aggregation strategy is unlikely to be a dominant remaining bottleneck within the multiprofile regime. It remains uncertain whether this small difference is statistically meaningful, whether other aggregation architectures or transformer hyperparameter tuning could yield larger gains, or whether further improvements are more likely to come from encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt) or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: Evidence: The multiprofile + avgpool + scvi_n200 configuration (config_005) achieved 0.650 accuracy, representing the largest gain so far (~13 pts over single-profile).
